7: [動詞]1 〈人が〉〈職業・希望・計画など〉を〔…のために〕(中途で)あきらめる, 断念[中止]する.2 〈人が〉〈家・国・船など〉を捨てる, 去る.3 〈妻・子・友人など〉を遺棄する；…を置き去りにする, 見捨てる.4 〈国・土地・城〉を〔…に〕引き渡す；…を〔…の〕なすがままにまかせる〔to, for〕.5 〔法律〕 〈財産・権利など〉を放棄する； 〈訴訟〉を取り下げる.6 〔保険〕(海上保険で)〈(船・貨物などの)保険に付された物〉を委付する.[名詞]放縦(ほうじゅう), 気まま中期英語 'abandone(n)'より遷移。古期フランス語 'abandoner'('ā bandon' 自分の自由裁量で)　からの借入語。　'ā'(atの意) はラテン語　'ad-'から派生。 ad- 「…へ」「…で」「…のそばで」の意味の印欧語根。重要な派生語は、at(1),aid, 接頭辞ad-を持つ単語（advice,announceなど）。 bhā-2 To speak.話すこと、宣言などを表す印欧語根。bee(1)の由来として、祈る者。abandon,banishなどの由来として、宣言。fame,famousなどの由来として、評判・名声。他の重要な派生語は、fatal, 語幹fessを持つ語（confess,professionalなど）など。 ad- 「…に向かって」, 「…へ」, の意。移動, 方向, 変化, 完成, 近似, 固着, 付加, 増加, 開始, 強意などを表す。"ad-" は　b, c, f, g, k, l, n, p, q, r, s, t の前では同化してそれぞれ　ab-, ac-, af-, ag-, ac-(k の前), al-, an-, ap-, ac-(q の前),ar-, as-, at-に置き換わる。「近似, 付加」の意味の時は通例　"ad-" (例：adscititious)。sc-, sp-, st-, gn- の前では　"a-" となる。 放棄する

etymology 1: From Middle English abandounen, from Old French abandoner, formed from a (“at, to”) + bandon (“jurisdiction, control”),[1] from Late Latin bannum (“proclamation”), bannus,[2] bandum, from Frankish *ban, *bann, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to proclaim, command”) (whence English ban), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”). See also ban, banal. Displaced Middle English forleten (“to abandon”), from Old English forlǣtan, anforlǣtan; see forlet; and Middle English forleven (“to leave behind, abandon”),  from Old English forlǣfan; see forleave. abandon (third-person singular simple present abandons, present participle abandoning, simple past and past participle abandoned) † Archaic or obsolete.
etymology 2: From Middle English abandoun, from Old French abandon, from Old French abondonner. abandon (countable and uncountable, plural abandons)

etymology 1: From Late Middle English abaishen, abashen, abaisse, abassen, abesse, abessen (“to be upset; to embarrass; to surprise; to confound; to bend down, stoop; to abase, degrade, disgrace”), from Middle French abaisser, from Old French abaissier, abessier (“to prostrate oneself; to lower, reduce”) (also compare Old French esbahir (“to amaze”), Vulgar Latin abbassiāre (“to lower”)),[1] from a- (prefix indicating movement towards something) (from Latin ad (“toward, to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at, to”)) + baissier (“to lower”) (from Medieval Latin bassus (“short of stature, low; base”), possibly from Ancient Greek βᾰ́σῐς (bắsĭs, “foot; base, foundation”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to step”)).[2][3] The spelling of the English word has been influenced by base, thus ostensibly analyzable as a- (“towards”) +‎ base.[4] There exist verb cognates in galloromance languages such as Catalan abaixar (“lower; abase”) and Occitan abaissar, and similar word construction in other romance languages as Spanish abajo (“down, downstairs; below”).

The English word was probably also influenced by the verb abate.[4] abate (third-person singular simple present abates, present participle abating, simple past and past participle abated)
etymology 3: Borrowed from Italian abate (“abbot”), from Latin abbātem, the accusative singular of abbās (“abbot”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), a variant of ἀββᾱ (abbā, “father; title of respect for an abbot”), from Aramaic אַבָּא (’abbā, “father; ancestor; teacher; chief, leader; author, originator”), from Proto-Semitic *ʔabw- (“father”), ultimately imitative of a child’s word for “father”. The verb was originally strong, conjugating for tense like take (e.g. I ake, I oke, I have aken), but gradually became weak during Middle English; the noun was originally pronounced as /eɪt͡ʃ/ as spelled (compare breach, from break). etymology 1: From Middle English affecten, from Latin affectāre, from Latin affectus, the participle stem of Latin afficere (“to act upon, influence, affect, attack with disease”), from ad- + facere (“to make, do”). affect (third-person singular simple present affects, present participle affecting, simple past and past participle affected) Affect and effect are sometimes confused. Affect conveys influence over something that already exists, but effect indicates the manifestation of new or original ideas or entities: The former indicates that major changes were made as a result of new policies, while the latter indicates that before new policies, major changes were in place, and that the new policies had some influence over these existing changes. The verbal noun uses of affect are distinguished from the verbal noun uses of effect more clearly than the regular verb forms. An affect is something that acts or acted upon something else. However, an effect is the result of an action (by something else).
etymology 2: From Middle English affecten, from Anglo-Norman affecter (“strive after”), Middle French affecter (“feign”), and their source, Latin affectāre (“to strive after, aim to do, pursue, imitate with dissimulation, feign”), frequentative of afficere (“to act upon, influence”) (see Etymology 1, above). affect (third-person singular simple present affects, present participle affecting, simple past and past participle affected)
etymology 3: From Middle English affect, from Latin affectus, adfectus (“a state of mind or body produced by some (external) influence, especially sympathy or love”), from afficere (“to act upon, influence”). affect (plural affects) Affect and effect can both be used as nouns or verbs, but when used as a noun the word affect is limited to the above psychology uses and the definitions for effect are much more common. See also the usage notes as a verb above.

etymology 1: From Late Middle English *amusen (“to mutter, be astonished, gaze meditatively on”), from Old French amuser (“to stupefy, waste time, be lost in thought”), from a- + muser (“to stare stupidly at, gape, wander, waste time, loiter, think carefully about, attend to”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Cognate with Occitan musa (“idle waiting”), Italian musare (“to gape idly about”). Possibly from Old French *mus (“snout”) from Vulgar Latin *mūsa (“snout”)  — compare Medieval Latin mūsum (“muzzle, snout”) –, from Proto-Germanic *mū- (“muzzle, snout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“lips, muzzle”). Compare North Frisian müs, mös (“mouth”), German Maul (“muzzle, snout”). Alternative etymology connects muser and musa with Frankish *muoza (“careful attention, leisure, idleness”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtǭ (“leave, permission”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to acquire, possess, control”). This would make it a cognate of Dutch musen (“to leisure”), Old High German *muoza (“careful attention, leisure, idleness”) and muozōn (“to be idle, have leisure or opportunity”), German Muße (“leisure”). etymology 1: Inherited from Middle English and, an, from Old English and, ond, end, from Proto-West Germanic *andi, from Proto-Germanic *andi, *anþi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti (“facing opposite, near, in front of, before”). Cognate with Scots an (“and”), North Frisian en (“and”), West Frisian en, in (“and”), Yiddish און (un, “and”), Low German un (“and”), Dutch en (“and”), German und (“and”), Danish end (“but”), Swedish än (“yet, but”), Icelandic and Norwegian enn (“still, yet”), Albanian edhe (“and”) (dialectal ênde, ênne), ende (“still, yet, therefore”), Latin ante (“opposite, in front of”), and Ancient Greek ἀντί (antí, “opposite, facing”). Doublet of  an ("if"). and Beginning a sentence with and or other coordinating conjunctions is considered incorrect by classical grammarians arguing that a coordinating conjunction at the start of a sentence has nothing to connect, but use of the word in this way is very common. The practice will be found in literature from Anglo-Saxon times onwards, especially as an aid to continuity in narrative and dialogue. The OED provides examples from the 9th century to the 19th century, including one from Shakespeare’s King John: “Arthur. Must you with hot Irons, burne out both mine eyes? Hubert. Young boy, I must. Arthur. And will you? Hubert. And I will.” It is also used for other rhetorical purposes, especially to denote surprise (O John! and you have seen him! And are you really going?—1884 in OED) and sometimes just to introduce an improvised afterthought (I’m going to swim. And don’t you dare watch—G. Butler, 1983) It is, however, poor style to separate short statements into separate sentences when no special effect is needed: I opened the door and I looked into the room (not *I opened the door. And I looked into the room). Combining sentences or starting with in addition or moreover is preferred in formal writing. And is often omitted for contextual effects of various kinds, especially between sequences of descriptive adjectives which can be separated by commas or simply by spaces (The teeming jerrybuilt dun-coloured traffic-ridden deafening city—Penelope Lively, 1987) In U.S. financial contexts such as check writing, and is often proscribed within full dollar amounts, reserved for use only immediately before the cent value. For instance, $150 is written "one hundred fifty", whereas "one hundred and fifty" is arguably ambiguous and could be taken to mean $100.50 instead. Some even teach that and literally means a decimal point, although a standard writing would at least denote the fractional dollar value as hundredths, e.g. with "/xx". and (plural ands)
etymology 2: Inherited from Middle English ande, from Old English anda (“grudge, enmity, malice, envy, hatred, anger, zeal, annoyance, vexation; zeal; injury, mischief; fear, horror”) and Old Norse andi (“breath, wind, spirit”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadô (“breath, anger, zeal”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”). Cognate with German Ahnd, And (“woe, grief”), Danish ånde (“breath”), Swedish anda, ande (“spirit, breath, wind, ingenuity, intellect”), Icelandic andi (“spirit”), Albanian ëndë (“pleasure, delight”), Latin animus (“spirit, soul”). The English word is analyzable as ante- +‎ diluvian. Sense 2 (“long extinct”) is from the fact that such animals and plants were originally believed to have perished in the biblical flood referred to above.[1]

etymology 1: From aster +‎ -oid, lit. "star-like". Coined by William Herschel. asteroid (plural asteroids) The term "asteroid" has never been precisely defined. It was coined for objects which looked like stars in a telescope but moved like planets. These were known from the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and were later found co-orbiting with Jupiter (Trojan asteroids) and within the orbit of Mars. They were naturally distinguished from comets, which did not look at all starlike. Starting in the 1970s, small non-cometary bodies were found outside the orbit of Jupiter, and usage became divided as to whether to call these "asteroids" as well. Some astronomers restrict the term "asteroid" to rocky or rocky-icy bodies with orbits up to Jupiter. They may retain the term planetoid for all small bodies, and thus tend to use it for icy or rocky-icy bodies beyond Jupiter, or may use dedicated words such as centaurs, Kuiper belt objects, transneptunian objects, etc. for the latter. Other astronomers use "asteroid" for all non-cometary bodies smaller than a planet, even large ones such as Sedna and (occasionally) Pluto. However, the distinction between asteroid and comet is an artificial one; many outer "asteroids" would become comets if they ventured nearer the Sun. The IAU terminology since 2006 has been small Solar System body for any body that orbits the Sun directly and whose shape is not dominated by gravity.

1384: (=azygosとも表記)[形容詞]単一性の[名詞]単一器官.「結合していない」というギリシャ語に由来 ne 広く否定の意味を表す印欧語根。重要な派生語は、no,not, 接頭辞a-1（awayなど）、接頭辞in-1（injuryなど）、接頭辞non-（nonentityなど）、接頭辞un-1（unlikeなど）などの単語。 yeug- 一緒になることを表す。 a-1 〔名詞・形容詞・副詞について〕「…と関係のない」「非…」「不…」not,withoutの意味を表す。　（母音および 'h' の前ではan-となる。） -zygous 「接合体構造を有する」の意の形容詞を作る.　例："heterozygous" (異形接合の)(語源) ギリシャ語　'-zugos' (つながれた)　←　'-zugos' (〔2頭の雄牛に掛ける〕くびき) に由来する。
New Latin, from Greek, unyoked, from a- + zygon yoke  — more at yoke

17605: [名]女性の人名(人名)(ギリシャ語 anastasis「復活」、文字通り「立ち上がること」より。ana「上へ、再び」+ histanai「立たせる」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17606: [名]染色体数が正常でないこと(異数性)(ギリシャ語 an-「〜でない」+ euploid〈eu「良い」+ -ploid、-ploos「折り畳み」に由来〉より)。(出典: etymonline)
17607: [名]微小な動物、特に微生物(後期ラテン語 animalculum、animal「生物」の指小形より)。(出典: etymonline)
17608: [名]併合、付加(中世ラテン語 annexatio「併合する行為」より。annexare「結びつける」〈ad「〜に」+ nectere「結ぶ、縛る」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17609: [名]「キリスト紀元」を意味するラテン語句、文字通り「主の年に」(annus「年」の奪格形 + 後期ラテン語 Domini「主の」〈Dominus「主」の属格〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17610: [名]無法状態、(神の)法への違反(フランス語 anomie より英語化。ギリシャ語 anomia「無法」、anomos「法のない」〈a-「〜なしに」+ nomos「法」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17611: [形]組織内の酸素欠乏を特徴とする、または引き起こす(医学ラテン語。ギリシャ語 an-「〜なしに」+ oxygen の最初の2文字 + -ic より)。(出典: etymonline)
17612: [名]ヘラクレスに倒されたリビュアの巨人(神名)(ギリシャ語 Antaios、文字通り「対立する、敵対する」より。anta「向かい合って」に由来し、anti「反対」と関連)。(出典: etymonline)
17613: [名]「正午前」を意味するラテン語句、文字通り「正午の前に」(ante「前に」+ meridies「正午」の対格形に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17614: [形]出産前に起こる、または存在する(ラテン語句 ante partum「出産前に」より。ante「前に」+ partus「出産」〈parire「産む」に由来〉)。(出典: etymonline)
17615: [動]実際より前の日付をつける、〜より年代が古い(ラテン語 ante「前に」+ date に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17616: [形]最後から3番目の(特に音節)(ラテン語 antepænultima「最後から2つ前の音節」の短縮形 antepenult より。ante「前に」+ pænultima〈pæne「ほとんど」+ ultima「最後」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17617: [名]神的存在に人間の感情を当てはめること(ギリシャ語 anthrōpopatheia「人間性」、文字通り「人間の感情」より。anthrōpos「人間」+ pathos「苦しみ、感情」に由来する -patheia)。(出典: etymonline)
17618: [名]地球の反対側(対蹠地)に住む人々(ラテン語 antichthontes より。ギリシャ語 antikhthōntēs「反対側の半球の人々」〈anti「反対の」+ khthōn「大地、土」〉に由来)。ピタゴラス哲学では地球の見えない分身を指した。(出典: etymonline)
17619: [名]オイディプスの娘(人名)。その名は「母の代わりに」を意味する可能性がある(ギリシャ語 anti「〜の代わりに」+ gonē「胎、出産、世代」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17620: [名]古代都市、現在のトルコのアンタキヤ(地名)。シリア王アンティオコスにちなんで名付けられた(ギリシャ語 Antiokhos、文字通り「抵抗する、持ちこたえる」より。anti「〜に対して」+ ekhein「持つ、保つ」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17621: [名]解熱剤(anti- + ギリシャ語 pyretos「熱、灼熱」〈pyr「火」に関連〉+ -ic に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17622: [名]古代ギリシャの合唱歌における一部分(対旋歌)(ギリシャ語 antistrophē「合唱隊の回帰」、文字通り「向きを変えること」より。anti「反対に、返して」+ strephein「回す」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17623: [形]地球の反対側に住む人々に関する(ギリシャ語 antoikoi、文字通り「向かい側の住人」より。anti「反対の」+ oikein「住む」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17624: [名]対義語(synonym「同義語」の対語として造られた。ギリシャ語 anti「反対の」+ onym「名前」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17625: [名]命題の反対を論駁することによる証明、帰謬法(ギリシャ語 apagogē「連れ去ること」より。apagein「連れ去る」〈apo「〜から離れて」+ agein「導く」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17626: [名]人付き合いへの嫌悪、孤独を好むこと(ギリシャ語 apanthrōpia より。apanthrōpos「非社交的な」〈apo「〜から離れて」+ anthrōpos「人間」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17627: [名]食欲を刺激するために食前に飲む酒(食前酒)(フランス語 apéritif「下剤、通じをよくする酒」、文字通り「開くもの」より。ラテン語 aperire「開く、覆いを取る」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17628: [名](毛穴・腸などを)開かせる薬、緩下剤(ラテン語 aperitivus より。aperire「開く、覆いを取る」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17629: [形]語頭の弱勢短母音の脱落によって生じた(言語学用語)(ギリシャ語 aphienai「手放す、送り出す」より。apo「〜から」+ hienai「送る、投げる」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17630: [形]声・音のない(ギリシャ語 aphonos「声のない」より。a-「〜なしに」+ phōnē「声」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17631: [形](深海域などが)日光の届かない、無光の(ギリシャ語 a-「〜なしに」+ phōs「光」の属格 phōtos + -ic に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17632: [名]『ヨハネの黙示録』に登場する底なし穴の破壊天使、悪魔の異名としても使われる(神名)(ギリシャ語 apollyein「完全に滅ぼす」の現在分詞より。apo + olluein「滅ぼす」に由来。ヘブライ語 Abaddon の訳語)。(出典: etymonline)
17633: [形]弁護・弁明を含む、後に「後悔して過失を認める」の意味も(ギリシャ語 apologetikos「弁護しうる」より。apologeisthai「自己弁護する」〈apo「〜から離れて」+ logos「言葉」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17634: [形]否定によって知識を得ることに関する、あるいは否定するふりをして言及すること(ギリシャ語 apophasis「否定」より。apophanai「言い放つ」〈apo「〜から離れて」+ phanai「話す」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17635: [名]神格化(特に皇帝や王族の)(ギリシャ語 apotheosis より。apotheoun「神にする」〈apo「変化」+ theos「神」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17636: [名]鎮静化、宥和(政策)(古フランス語 apaisement「なだめること」より。apaisier「なだめる、和平をもたらす」に由来)。1919年に国際政治用語となり、1939年のチェンバレン首相の対独政策の失敗後に否定的な意味を帯びた。(出典: etymonline)
17637: [名]強い欲求、渇望(フランス語 appétence より。ラテン語 appetentia「何かを渇望すること」〈appetere「求める」、ad「〜へ」+ petere「求める」〉に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17638: [形]翅(はね)のない(a-「〜なしに」+ ギリシャ語 pteryx「翅」に由来する pterous)。(出典: etymonline)
17639: [名]精製前のアルコールを指す錬金術用語、文字通り「生命の水」。後にブランデーやウイスキーにも用いられた(ラテン語 aqua「水」+ vitae「生命の」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17640: [名]水中で呼吸するための携帯式空気タンクと器具(aqua-「水」+ lung「肺」に由来)。1943年にジャック・クストーとエミール・ガニャンにより開発された。(出典: etymonline)
17641: [名]星座および黄道十二宮の第11番目(みずがめ座)(ラテン語 aquarius、文字通り「水を運ぶ者」より。ギリシャ語 Hydrokhoos「水を注ぐ者」の翻訳借用)。(出典: etymonline)
17642: [形]水の性質を持つ、水を多く含む(ラテン語 aqua「水」より、フランス語 aqueux「水っぽい」に類推して形成)。(出典: etymonline)
17643: [名]水を含んだ地層(帯水層)(ラテン語 aqui-「水」+ -fer「運ぶもの」〈ferre「運ぶ」に由来〉)。(出典: etymonline)
17644: [名]フランス南西部の歴史的な公国(地名)(ラテン語 Aquitania より。第一要素は aqua「水」、第二要素はおそらく「土地、地方」を意味する)。(出典: etymonline)
17645: [名]化学元素アルゴン(ギリシャ語 argos「怠惰な、働かない」の中性形 argon より。a-「〜なしに」+ ergon「仕事」に由来)。不活性な性質にちなんで発見者が命名した。(出典: etymonline)
17646: [名]アルゴ船の乗組員(神話上の英雄たち)(Argo〈船の名〉+ ギリシャ語 nautēs「船乗り」に由来)。1848年のカリフォルニア・ゴールドラッシュの冒険者たちもこう呼ばれた。(出典: etymonline)
17647: [名]最良の人々による統治(賢人政治)(ギリシャ語 aristarkhia より。aristos「最良の」+ -arkhia「統治」に由来)。「厳格な批評」の意味は、ホメロス作品の注釈者アリスタルコスの人名に由来する。(出典: etymonline)
17648: [名]腕輪、腕環(ラテン語 armilla「腕輪」より。armus「肩、上腕」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17649: [名]ブルターニュの古称(地名)(ガロ・ローマ語 Aremorica、文字通り「海の前」より。「〜の前」を意味するケルト語の接頭辞 + mare「海」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17650: [名]武器類の総称、防具/武器を製造・保管する場所(武器庫)。また「紋章学」の意味もある(古フランス語 armoierie「紋章術」〈armoier「紋章を描く」、ラテン語 arma「武器」に由来〉)。(出典: etymonline)
17651: [名]動脈硬化症(医学ラテン語。arterio-「動脈の」+ sclerosis「硬化症」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17652: [名]関節の痛み。1848年、それ以前に仏語・独語で使用。ギリシャ語 arthron「関節」(PIE語根 *ar-「組み合わさる」に由来)+ -algia「痛み」から。(出典: etymonline)
17653: [名]関節のある脚を持つ無脊椎動物。1862年、近代ラテン語 Arthropoda(文字通り「関節のある足を持つもの」)から。(出典: etymonline)
17654: [名]節足動物門。1849年、近代ラテン語。ギリシャ語 arthron「関節」(PIE語根 *ar-「組み合わさる」)+ pous「足」の属格 podos(PIE語根 *ped-「足」)から。(出典: etymonline)
17655: [名]関節に細い管を挿入して行う関節疾患の外科的処置。1977年、arthro-「関節」+ -scopy「観察」から。(出典: etymonline)
17656: [名]書き加えること、また著作や起源を特定の人・ものに帰すること。1590年代、ラテン語 ascriptio「書き加え」から。ラテン語 ascribere「書き加える、帰する」(ad「〜へ」+ scribere「書く」、PIE語根 *skribh-「切る」)に由来。(出典: etymonline)
17657: [名](法律)物を運び去ること、窃取。1500年頃、ラテン語 asportatio「運び去ること」から。asportare「運び去る」(abs-「離れて」+ portare「運ぶ」、PIE語根 *per- (2)「導く、通り過ぎる」)に由来。(出典: etymonline)
17658: [名]1530年代「(債務を弁済するに)十分な財産」の意。後に「財産、特に換金可能な財産」の意に(1580年代)。古フランス語 assez「十分」、俗ラテン語 *ad satis「十分に」(ad「〜へ」+ satis「十分」、PIE語根 *sa-「満足させる」)に由来。(出典: etymonline)
17659: [名]スペイン王と他国との間の契約、特に1713年ユトレヒト条約でイギリスにアフリカ人奴隷供給を認めた契約。スペイン語 asiento「契約、席」に由来し、原義は「席に着かせること」。ラテン語 sedere「座る」(PIE語根 *sed- (1)「座る」)から。(出典: etymonline)
17660: [名]共通の目的のために集まること、団体。1530年代、中世ラテン語 associatio から。associare「結びつける」(ad「〜へ」+ sociare「結合する」、socius「仲間」、PIE語根 *sekw- (1)「従う」に由来)。「精神的な連想」の意は1680年代から。(出典: etymonline)
17661: [形]不安定な、定位置を持たない。1827年、ギリシャ語 astatos「不安定な」(a-「〜でない」+ statos「立った」、PIE語根 *sta-「立つ」)から。(出典: etymonline)
17662: [名]放射性元素。1947年命名。ギリシャ語 astatos「不安定な」+ 化学接尾辞 -ine から。安定同位体を持たない短半減期に由来する。(出典: etymonline)
17663: [名]地球上部マントルの層。1914年、文字通り「弱さの球」の意。ギリシャ語 asthenes「弱い」+ sphere「球」から。(出典: etymonline)
17664: [名]宇宙生物学。1903年、フランス語 astrobiologie から。astro-「星」+ biology「生物学」。(出典: etymonline)
17665: [名]恒星の名称・等級などに関する知識。1835年、astro-「星」+ -gnosy(ギリシャ語 gnōsis「知識」、PIE語根 *gno-「知る」に由来)から。(出典: etymonline)
17666: [形]星形の。1909年、ギリシャ語 astroeides から。astron「星」(PIE語根 *ster- (2)「星」)+ -oeidēs「〜の形をした」。1897年には名詞としても使われた。(出典: etymonline)
17667: [名]天体崇拝。1670年代、astro-「星」+ -latry「崇拝」から。(出典: etymonline)
17668: [名]星占い、星や惑星の人間への神秘的影響を判断する術。1650年代、astro-「星」+ -mancy「〜による占い」から。(出典: etymonline)
17669: [名]人工芝の商標名。1966年、ヒューストンのアストロドームで最初に使用されたことに由来。astro-「星、宇宙」+ turf「芝」から。ヒューストンは米国宇宙計画の管制センター所在地だった。(出典: etymonline)
17670: [名]肺の不完全な拡張。1836年、医学ラテン語。ギリシャ語 atelēs「不完全な」+ ektosis「伸展」(ek「〜から外へ」+ teinein「伸ばす」、PIE語根 *ten-「伸ばす」)から。(出典: etymonline)
17671: [形]神を信じない、不敬な。1610年代、ラテン語 atheus、ギリシャ語 atheos から。a-「〜でない」+ theos「神」(PIE語根 *dhes-「宗教概念を表す語を形成する」)。1880年からは「神の存在を考慮しない」の意でも使われた。(出典: etymonline)
17672: [名]中央の礁湖を囲むサンゴの帯状・環状の島。1620年代、マラヤーラム語 atolu「礁」から。adal「閉じる、結合する」に由来するとされる。ワトキンズはサンスクリット語 antara-「内部」(PIE語根 *en「中に」)に遡る可能性を指摘。(出典: etymonline)
17673: [名]ベラドンナから得られる有毒な結晶性アルカロイド。1831年、ラテン語 atropa「ベラドンナ」から。ギリシャ語 atropos「変えられない」(運命の女神の一人の名でもある)+ 化学接尾辞 -ine。(出典: etymonline)
17674: [名]初期には「やせ衰えること」、食事については「減量」の意。ラテン語 attenuatio から。attenuare「薄くする、減じる」(ad「〜へ」+ tenuare「薄くする」、tenuis「薄い」、PIE語根 *ten-「伸ばす」に由来)。1590年代から「密度を薄くすること」の一般的な意味、1838年から電流にも使われた。(出典: etymonline)
17675: [形]増大させる力・性質を持つ。1500年頃、古フランス語 augmentatif から。後期ラテン語 augmentare「増やす」に由来。文法用語としては1640年代から、意味を強める語や接辞を指す。(出典: etymonline)
17676: [名]男性の人名。ラテン語 augustus「尊厳ある」に由来。もとはガイウス・ユリウス・カエサル・オクタウィアヌスが皇帝として名乗った称号で、「陛下」に近い意味合いだった。(出典: etymonline)
17677: [形]old の異形で、アングロサクソン語の母音をより忠実に残す。北イングランドおよびスコットランドの方言に残存し、14世紀末以降は特にスコットランド語形となった。(出典: etymonline)
17678: [名]鳥の飛び方を観察して吉凶を占う者。1590年代、ラテン語 auspex から。PIE *awi-spek-「鳥を観察する者」(語根 *awi-「鳥」+ 語根 *spek-「観察する」)に由来。(出典: etymonline)
17679: [名]もとは鳥占いによる予兆観察(1530年代)。1650年代に「未来の兆し」、1630年代には「後援、庇護」の意(under the auspices of の形で)に広がった。ラテン語 auspicium に由来。(出典: etymonline)
17680: [名]異端審問所が下す判決、特に異端者の公開火刑。1723年、ポルトガル語 auto-da-fé「信仰の行為」(ラテン語 actus de fide)から。fides「信仰」は PIE語根 *bheidh-「信頼する、説得する」に由来。(出典: etymonline)
17681: [形]その土地に生まれた、土着の。1827年、autochthon + -ic から。(出典: etymonline)
17682: [名]蒸気自体で蓋が密閉される調理・滅菌装置。1847年、フランス語から。文字通り「自己施錠」の意で、auto-「自己」+ clave(ラテン語 clavis「鍵」、PIE語根 *klau-「鉤」に由来)。(出典: etymonline)
17683: [形]自ら生成された。1846年(それ以前は1650年代に autogeneal)、ギリシャ語 autogenetos「自ら生まれた」(autos「自己」+ genetos「生まれた」、PIE語根 *gene-「生む」に由来)から。(出典: etymonline)
17684: [名]自治の状態、自治権。1620年代、国家について用いられた。ギリシャ語 autonomia「独立」から。autonomos「自らの法で生きる」(autos「自己」+ nomos「慣習、法」、PIE語根 *nem-「割り当てる」に由来)。個人については1803年から。(出典: etymonline)
17685: [名]フランス語で文字通り「前衛部隊」の意。15〜18世紀に英語で軍事的な意味で使われ、1910年に「ある時代の先駆者・革新者」を指す芸術用語として再導入された。(出典: etymonline)
17686: [名]航空機の操縦士。1887年、フランス語 aviateur から。ラテン語 avis「鳥」(PIE語根 *awi-「鳥」)+ -ateur。(出典: etymonline)

English America
Learned borrowing from New Latin America, feminine Latinized form of the Italian first name of Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512). Amerigo is an Italian name derived from a Germanic language and is etymologically related to Henry and Emmerich. The earliest known use of America for the (South) American continent is on a 1507 map by Martin Waldseemüller; see Naming of the Americas for more.
Although this is the most widely accepted derivation, it has also been suggested that it could originate from the name of the Amerrisque mountains in Nicaragua (from Mayan), and another disputed theory is that it derives from the surname of Richard Amerike (1440–1503), whose surname is an anglicised form of Welsh ap Meurig (“son of Meurig”), from Old Welsh Mouric, which could be a rendition of Latin Mauritius (compare Maurice).

The modern North American and Australasian usage, referring to East and Southeast Asians collectively, seems to be a shortened form of "Asian American", a term whose origins activists and academics trace back to 1968 and University of California, Berkeley (UCLA) students Yuji Ichioka and Emma Gee, who, inspired by the Black Power Movement and the protests against the Vietnam War, founded the "Asian American Political Alliance" as a way to unite Japanese, Chinese, and Filipino American students on campus. It replaced the term "Mongoloid", but still continued the racial grouping of "Mongoloid".
The usage in Britain and some of its former colonies such as South Africa, Kenya and Uganda, stems from South Asians historically forming the bulk of immigrants from the continent of Asia to these places.
In the rest of the Anglosphere, the word "Asian" is sometimes, albeit less frequently, used to refer to South Asians and Central Asians, but rarely (if ever) to Near Easterners.

Wiktionary: First attested in the 15th century from Middle English alcofol, from Middle French alcohol or Spanish alcohol, derived from the Medieval Latin rendering alcohol transmitted in medical or alchemical literature of Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”), which in Andalusian Arabic also bore the form كُحُول (kuḥūl), قُحُول (quḥūl); bearing thus the meaning of stibnite first, then generalized in meaning to a powder obtained by triturating a material, then also to liquids obtained by boiling down, and specialized to mean spirit of wine, ethanol, in the 18th century, then the narrow chemical sense after 1850. Doublet of alcool and kohl.
Various old etymological notes.
* Bartholomew Traheron in his 1543 translation of John of Vigo introduces the word as a term used by "barbarous" (Moorish) authors for "fine powder": the barbarous auctours use alcohol, or (as I fynde it sometymes wryten) alcofoll, for moost fine poudre.
* William Johnson in his 1657 Lexicon Chymicum glosses the word as antimonium sive stibium. By extension, the word came to refer to any fluid obtained by distillation, including "alcohol of wine", the distilled essence of wine.
* Libavius in Alchymia (1594) has vini alcohol vel vinum alcalisatum.
* Johnson (1657) glosses alcohol vini as quando omnis superfluitas vini a vino separatur, ita ut accensum ardeat donec totum consumatur, nihilque fæcum aut phlegmatis in fundo remaneat.
* Some authorities, including Rachel Hajar, suggest that the ultimate etymon was the Arabic term اَلْغَوْل (al-ḡawl, “bad effect, evil result of headache”) (as used in Qur’an verse 37:47, but this word is rather poetical and could for topical reasons not have been picked up from Arabic by Medieval writers, and aside from that the relation to stibium is well documented.

20296: Sanskrit ārya noble, belonging to an ancient people of northern India speaking an Indo-European dialect

Wiktionary: Originally from Sanskrit आर्य (ā́rya, “noble; noble one”) and + -n. The Sanskrit word is an autonym originally from Proto-Indo-Iranian *áryas (see there for more). Borrowed into English in the 19th century, at first as a term for the Indo-Iranian languages, and later partly extended to the Indo-European languages and peoples following a theory by Friedrich Schlegel that connected the Indo-Iranian words arya/ā́rya with German Ehre (“honor”) and some older Germanic names, thus assuming that it was the original Indo-European autonym meaning "the honorable people". The original meaning of the Indo-Iranian autonym and its possible Indo-European origin/cognates are disputed (see the Wikipedia article for further details).
The same Proto-Indo-Iranian root is the ultimate source of the country name Iran. Also the doublet of Arya.

Wiktionary: From Middle English ah, aa, a (“ah”), of imitative origin, or from Old English ēa, *eah (“oh, alas”), from Proto-West Germanic *a, *ah (“ah”). Earliest recorded use is circa 1175 in the Ormulum: A, Maȝȝstre! icc wat tatt tu full wiss Arrt Godess Sune ("Ah, Master! I know for sure that thou art God's Son"). Some propose that the Middle English is borrowed from Old French a (“ah!, oh!, hey!”) (represented by modern French ah).
Compare also West Frisian a, ah (“ah”), Dutch a, ah (“ah”), Middle Low German a (“ah”), Old High German a, aa, ah (“ah, oh”) (whence modern German ah), Faroese áh (“oh, ah, alas”), Icelandic æ, ai (“ah, oh”), Latin ah (“ah”).

Wiktionary: According to Etymology Online, the term was first attested in 1706 meaning am not, and it was used with that sense until the early 19th century, when it began to be used as a generic contraction for are not, is not, etc. in the Cockney dialect. It was then “popularized by representations of London cockney dialect in Dickens, etc., which led to the word being banished […] from correct English”.
The shift from /ænt/ to /eɪnt/ parallels a similar change some dialects made to can't. In other dialects, the pronunciation shifted to /ɑːnt/, and the spelling aren't, when used to mean “am not”, is due to the fact that both words are pronounced /ɑːnt/ in some non-rhotic dialects. Historically, ain't was present in many dialects of the English language, but not in the southeastern England dialect that became the standard, where it is only found in the construction ain't I. It has become widely known through modern media, although it is much more common in some areas of the English-speaking world than others (e.g. it is less common in Yorkshire).
As a contraction of have not and has not, ain't derives from the earlier form han't, which shifted from /hænt/ to /heɪnt/, and underwent h-dropping in most dialects.

24935:
Wiktionary: From a clipping of Australian (or Australia) + -ie.
The spelling likely adopted the visual template of the pre‐existing personal diminutive Aussie (from Austin or Augusta). However, while the personal nickname retains standard English phonics with a voiceless /s/, the pronunciation of the national slang (/ˈɒzi/) was driven by a highly productive morphophonological template in Commonwealth slang that strongly favors short stressed vowels and lenited consonants.
The clipped base promotes the historically unstressed initial vowel to the short /ɒ/. This reflects a broader Commonwealth phonological rule where the /ɔː/ typically associated with the ⟨au⟩ digraph is shortened before a tautosyllabic /s/ or /s/‐cluster (as in austral). To lock in this short vowel on the page and prevent readers from reverting to an open‐syllable pronunciation, writers doubled the s as a structural dummy consonant.
This created an orthographic trap. The spelling effectively represents a conservative /ˈɔːsi/, preserving the standard phonetic values of both the long vowel and the voiceless fricative. However, the egalitarian colloquial register actively demanded the lenited (voiced) /z/ (compare Tassie, Brissie, possie, cossie). Thus, the dialect compromised by writing the conservative, etymological ⟨ss⟩, while speaking the colloquial /z/.
Though popularized internationally as military slang from 1915 onwards, early printed evidence shows the clipping was already active in Australian sporting vernacular by at least 1913.

Wiktionary: From Middle English alighten (“to descend from a place: to dismount, get off; to descend to a place: to arrive or stop (at a place); to land; to drop; to attack; of lightning: to strike; to leap on to, mount; to descend in rank; to cause (someone) to lose rank; to come forth, spring from; to alleviate, relieve; (Christianity) of Jesus: to come down to earth from heaven, become incarnate; to descend (to hell); of the Holy Spirit, angels, miracles, etc.: to descend (from heaven); to descend (upon someone); to appear in a place”) [and other forms], from a merger of:
* Old English ālīhtan (“to alight, dismount”), from ā- (prefix meaning ‘away, from, off, out’) + līhtan, līehtan (“to descend, alight, light; to make easy or light, alleviate, lighten, relieve”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“not heavy, light”); and
* Old English ġelīhtan (“to descend; to come down, dismount; to make easy or light, alleviate, lighten, relieve”), from ġe- (intensifying prefix, attached to verbs to indicate completeness or perfection) + līhtan, līehtan (see above).
The English word is analyzable as a- (prefix meaning ‘away, from, off, out’) + light (“to ease, lighten; to take off; to unload; to dismount; (archaic) to come down, land; to dismount”).
Cognates
* Middle Low German erlichten (“to lighten”)
* Old High German gilīhten (“to make less heavy, lighten”) (Middle High German gelīhten); Old High German irlīhten (“to alleviate”) (Middle High German erlīhten, modern German erleichten)
